Interactive Playmat for Toddlers

A low-cost, screen-free playmat that responds to a child's steps with light and sound, and gives caregivers a way to monitor play. Final year project, BE Mechatronics (2023–2027), Air University.

Context
Final year project, Department of Mechatronics & Biomedical Engineering, Air University, Islamabad
Team
Huzairah Fatima, Ahram Khan, Maryam Shamyl Nasir
Supervision
Dr. Syed Hammad Nazeer Gilani (supervisor), Dr. Fizza Farukh (co-supervisor)
My role
Lead on requirement analysis and research, component selection, mechanism selection and system integration (per the report's work division).
Status
Not final yet, about 70% complete

The problem

Traditional playmats are passive: they look good but don't respond to what a child does. That limits cause-and-effect learning and exploration through feedback.

Existing interactive solutions are expensive, complex, or lack real-time feedback and caregiver control. The report points out that in countries like Pakistan, access to modern interactive toys is limited by cost and supply.

Problem statement (from the report)

Conventional play mats are passive and fail to support active learning and motor development. Existing interactive solutions are expensive, complex, or lack real-time feedback and caregiver control. There are few affordable systems that combine pressure sensing, audiovisual interaction and remote monitoring in a single platform.

Who it's for

  • Toddlers: the report targets young children, with the literature gap framed around ages 6–36 months.
  • Caregivers: they need simple control of game modes and a view of basic interaction data (a planned Android app in the report).

The solution

A mat divided into pressure-sensitive zones. A force-sensing resistor (FSR) in each zone detects a step, crawl or press, and an ESP32 microcontroller identifies the active zone and triggers LED and audio feedback. Wi-Fi lets a caregiver app switch game modes, adjust sensitivity and see activity.

  • Design real-time audiovisual feedback through LEDs and sound to increase engagement.
  • Develop a mobile app for monitoring and control.
  • Analyse interaction data such as response time and activity patterns, while keeping the system low-cost and safe. The report states this is not a diagnostic tool.

Product thinking behind the design

Cause and effect

Every press gets an immediate light and sound response, so the child learns that their action made it happen.

Reliable detection

Per-sensor calibration, thresholds, filtering and debouncing stop noise and accidental touches from triggering the system.

Caregiver in control

Game modes, light and sound output and sensor sensitivity are meant to be adjustable from the app without interrupting play.

Affordable by design

The report's estimated parts cost is Rs 15,600, using common modules such as the ESP32 and FSR 402 sensors.

System design

The report describes layers for power, sensing, processing, output, communication, the mobile app and data monitoring. The flow chart shows the loop: read the four FSRs, compare against a threshold, identify the zone, trigger light and sound, notify the app if connected, then wait for release.

Simulation (MATLAB Simulink / Simscape)

I modelled the electronics and controller logic before building. In the model, four force inputs and four IR object states feed a MATLAB function block that stands in for the ESP32. It outputs seven relay triggers (red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, white LEDs) and two audio triggers for the speakers.

  • FSR input stage: modelled as a voltage divider with a 10 kΩ pull-down.
  • IR input stage: digital, 0 = object clear and 1 = object detected (0 V / 5 V).
  • Relay and LED stage: digital signal to an SPST relay, with a 470 Ω resistor in series with each LED.
  • Audio stage: MAX98357A I2S amplifier driving a 4 Ω speaker load, monitored with a scope.

Schematic design

The schematic connects an ESP32 DevKit to four FSRs, four IR sensors, an 8-channel relay module driving seven indicator LEDs, and two MAX98357 audio modules with speakers.

FSR1–FSR4D34, D35, D32, D33
